title: What will today’s money become?
lead: Meridian can set aside $1,000 for one year at 6% simple interest.
prompt: Use future value to plan a future balance or a loan repayment.
notes: Explain the 1 before multiplying. It represents 100% of the original principal; rt is the additional fraction earned.

title: Work backward from the interest earned
lead: Meridian earned $60 at 6% over one year. How much was originally invested?
prompt: Use this when the interest is known but the original investment is missing.
notes: Distinguish interest I from total future value FV. Optional algebra: r=I/(P×t); t=I/(P×r).

title: What would you pay today for $1,060 later?
lead: Meridian is offered a $1,060 receipt in one year. Its comparable simple return is 6%.
prompt: Discounting finds the starting money needed to produce a promised future amount.
notes: Explain division as reversing multiplication. A higher future receipt is not automatically a better offer.

title: Try it: separate the money from its earnings
lead: Use the $1,000, 6%, one-year example in your follow-along.
prompt: Calculate interest first, then the whole balance. Why are these different amounts?

title: The original money does not disappear
lead: A 6% return adds six cents for every dollar held for a full year.
prompt: Future value = principal + interest. Quoting only $60 leaves out the original investment.
notes: The small interest segment is proportional to the original principal. Connect the 6% rate to the size of the addition.

title: Two questions can point to the same starting money
lead: One starts with the earnings. The other starts with the entire future receipt.
prompt: Try both backward calculations. Choose the formula from what the question gives you.

title: Same answer, different information
lead: Both calculations describe the same investment under the same simple-interest assumptions.
prompt: Never divide interest by the total growth factor, or divide the whole receipt by the interest rate alone.

title: Could a short loan solve a cash shortage?
lead: Meridian borrows $18,500 for 8 months at 6.2% annual simple interest.
prompt: Build checkpoint B, then explain how much of the repayment is interest.
location: Live You Try It · G12:G14; explanation B31:G33

title: Budget for the whole repayment
lead: The annual rate applies to only eight months of borrowing.
prompt: The borrowing cost is $764.67. The cash required at maturity is $19,264.67.

title: Days are another way to describe the wait
lead: Meridian’s short-term note runs for 80 actual days.
prompt: The contract’s year basis tells you how to convert the days before calculating interest.

title: Same loan. Same days. Two possible conventions.
lead: Compare 75-day interest on $42,000 at a 4.8% annual rate.
prompt: Predict which produces more interest. Then calculate checkpoint A and explain why.
location: Live You Try It · G6:G10; explanation B26:G28

title: A slightly larger year fraction means more interest
lead: The annual rate, principal, and actual waiting period all stay the same.
prompt: Use the agreed convention. The two calculations differ because their denominators differ.

title: Does the interest earn interest too?
lead: Start with the same $1,000 and 6% annual rate. Now hold it for two years.
prompt: The extra $3.60 is 6% earned on the prior $60 of interest.
notes: Predict the second-year interest before explaining the second lane. Growth formulas are simple FV=P(1+rt) and compound FV=P(1+r)^t.

title: The growth rule determines the discount rule
lead: What is $1,120 received in two years worth today at 6%?
prompt: Discounting reverses the stated growth process. It does not choose the process for you.

title: A negative PV can describe a valuable investment
lead: From the investor’s viewpoint, money leaves today and comes back later.
prompt: For comparing offers, show the positive magnitude with −PV(…). Keep the investor’s direction clear.

title: A good valuation makes the round trip
lead: If today’s value is correct, growing it forward should recover the promised receipt.
prompt: Use the same rate, time, and model in both directions. Excel’s FV function provides the same check.

title: What should Meridian pay for a future receipt?
lead: A client offers $30,000 payable in two years. Meridian requires 6.5% annually.
prompt: Build checkpoint C. Explain the cash-flow signs and what your verification confirms.
location: Live You Try It · G16:G18; explanation B36:G38

title: The discount creates room to earn the return
lead: A smaller investment today can grow into the $30,000 future receipt.
prompt: In Excel: the investment is a negative outflow; its comparison value is a positive magnitude.

title: A 15-month wait is more than one annual period
lead: Meridian expects $18,000 in 15 months at a 6% annual compound rate.
prompt: The exponent uses annual periods. This example assumes fractional-year annual compound discounting.

title: A longer wait means more discounting
lead: At a fixed 6% annual rate, compare the same $100 received on three dates.
prompt: Practical use: compare payment schedules. A later receipt must compensate you for waiting longer.

title: What return would make waiting worthwhile?
lead: For $100 received in three years, a higher required return means a lower value today.
prompt: Practical use: ask whether the payment’s timing and risk justify the price you pay today.
notes: Connect the required return to opportunity cost, purchasing power and payment risk without mechanically adding three percentages.

title: Find the most valuable corner
lead: Value today of $100 received later. Across: change the wait. Down: change the required return.
prompt: Shortest wait + lowest rate gives the highest PV. Explain the pattern, then recreate it in the workbook.

title: Choose the model that matches the promise
lead: Meridian expects $18,000 in two years at 6%. Which rule belongs in the denominator?
prompt: The challenge specifies annual compounding. Use that model consistently for every payment.

title: One future payment becomes one value today
lead: Worked example: a $10,000 payment due at the end of year 2; required annual return 6%.
prompt: Practical use: value an invoice, contract payment, or other future receipt on today’s date.

title: Which offer would you accept?
lead: Meridian can choose $75,000 today or five future receipts. Use a 6% annual compound rate.
prompt: Value every receipt today before comparing. Build the challenge, then make and defend your choice.

title: Different payment dates, one comparison date
lead: Each receipt is discounted for its own waiting period.
prompt: Do not add future dollars first and discount them as if they all arrive together.

title: The payment stream has the higher value today
lead: At the stated 6% rate, compare the two offers on the same date.
prompt: A higher required return or less reliable future payments could reverse the recommendation.

title: Use the formula to answer a business question
lead: The model turns payment timing into a decision you can explain.
prompt: Before calculating: identify the known amount, the unknown, the growth model, and the valuation date.
